abstract: Clp proteases are central to bacterial proteostasis, yet our biochemical understanding of actinobacterial Clp enzymes derives almost entirely from mycobacteria, where their essentiality complicates efforts to understand their physiological behavior. Here, we reconstitute and biochemically characterize the ClpCP1P2 protease from Corynebacterium glutamicum, a genetically tractable actinobacterium in which clpC and clpX are non-essential. We find that, as in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, ClpP1 and ClpP2 are individually inactive and form an active peptidase only when stabilized by ATP-bound ClpC or acyldepsipeptide antibiotics, with further stimulation by N-blocked peptide agonists. However, C. glutamicum ClpCP1P2 exhibits faster kinetics and greater conformational stability than its mycobacterial orthologs, proteolyzing full-length substrates rapidly without requiring peptide agonists. We additionally show that the anti-mycobacterial antibiotics rufomycin and cyclomarin A bind the C. glutamicum ClpC N-terminal domain, exert substrate-specific effects on proteolysis, and impair C. glutamicum growth. The ability of these compounds to elicit toxicity through a non-essential target suggests that they act via gain-of-function dysregulation rather than simple inhibition. Together, our results validate C. glutamicum as a tractable model for interrogating Actinomycetota Clp proteases.
